title: Economic and Financial Learning with Artificial Intelligence: A Mixed-Methods Study on ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper examines how learners perceive and use ChatGPT as an educational tool for economic and financial learning, with particular attention to changes in attitudes before and after direct exposure. The study addresses three main questions: how users perceive ChatGPT prior to use, how those perceptions shift after use, and what benefits, challenges, and improvement needs emerge when learners use ChatGPT for learning. The paper is motivated by the growing interest in AI chatbots in education and the need for empirical evidence beyond theoretical claims.

The intervention was a structured pretest-posttest learning session in which participants first completed a questionnaire about their demographics, prior chatbot experience, expectations, and concerns. They then used ChatGPT to learn self-selected business and economics topics, with prompting guidance provided at the outset and expert observers present to monitor progress, challenges, and content quality. After the session, participants completed a second questionnaire and open-ended reflections. The study combined quantitative Likert-scale survey data with qualitative feedback from participants and experimenters, making it a mixed-methods investigation of both perceptions and reported learning experiences.

The sample included 102 participants ranging in age from 8 to 79. Reported occupations included 60 school students, 22 university students, and 19 employed adults, so the study spans multiple learner groups rather than a single educational level. The context was short, supervised ChatGPT-based learning sessions focused on economics and business topics; average total session time was 52 minutes. The text does not identify a specific school, institution, or country. Outcomes were based primarily on self-reported perceptions of competence, enjoyment, helpfulness, response quality, and understanding, supplemented by observer notes and identification of a small number of potentially misconception-inducing errors in ChatGPT responses.

The main conclusion is that even brief exposure to ChatGPT in a guided learning context can substantially improve learners' perceptions of chatbots for education, especially perceived competence and enjoyment of learning with the tool. Participants generally found ChatGPT helpful, interactive, and efficient, and post-exposure ratings were strongly positive. However, the study also identifies important challenges, especially crafting effective prompts, evaluating answer trustworthiness, lack of sources, verbosity, occasional inaccuracies, and limited visual support. The author argues that these findings support the development of an 'AI-learning-competence' framework and suggests that formal educational integration and training may help learners use AI tools more effectively and critically.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for interactive question-answering, explanations, and personalized learning support.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants used ChatGPT during guided sessions to learn self-selected economics and business topics, with pre/post questionnaires assessing perceptions, experiences, and self-reported learning outcomes; some participants used GPT-4 and others GPT-3.5, normalized here to ChatGPT.

findings.finding_summary: After the ChatGPT learning session, participants reported high self-rated topic understanding (M = 4.1, SD = 0.9), and found ChatGPT's responses helpful (M = 4.3, SD = 0.9) and high quality (M = 4.2, SD = 1.0). These are self-reported learning-related outcomes from 102 participants studying economics/business topics.
findings.measure: Self-reported topic understanding, helpfulness of ChatGPT responses, and perceived response quality on 5-point scales

findings.finding_summary: Post-session ratings showed marked improvements in perceptions related to using ChatGPT, especially perceived competence using chatbots (+0.74) and enjoyment derived from learning with chatbots (+0.66). Other positive shifts included quality of responses (+0.52), improve learning (+0.55), usage in class (+0.45), and feeling comfortable (+0.37).
findings.measure: Pre/post Likert-scale perception shifts regarding competence, enjoyment, comfort, and perceived learning value
findings.effect_size: Δ-Mean competence=+0.74; fun-learning=+0.66; response quality=+0.52; improve learning=+0.55; usage in class=+0.45; comfort=+0.37

findings.finding_summary: Male participants rated ChatGPT higher than females on the perception that it could improve learning: males M = 4.31 (SD = 0.7) versus females M = 3.83 (SD = 1.1), t(92) = 2.458, p = 0.02, with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 0.95). This reflects a subgroup difference in perceived learning benefit rather than an overall treatment effect.
findings.measure: Perceived potential of ChatGPT to improve learning

findings.finding_summary: Participants using ChatGPT via GPT-4 reported significantly better experiences than those using GPT-3.5 across multiple perception measures. Reported effects included general enjoyment (d = 0.908, p = 0.010), insecurity (d = 1.053, p = 0.018), comfort (d = 0.977, p = 0.012), clarity of responses (d = 0.897, p = 0.018), response quality (d = 0.757, p = 0.032), enjoyment of learning (d = 0.951, p < 0.001), desire for classroom use (d = 1.121, p = 0.006), and perceived potential to enhance learning (d = 0.936, p = 0.002).
findings.measure: Post-session Likert ratings comparing GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5 experiences

findings.finding_summary: Across 230 distinct economics/business topics explored with ChatGPT, experimenters detected five errors with potential to create misconceptions, relating to types of goods, economic principles, and economies of scope. At the same time, participants overwhelmingly appreciated the explanations and speed of support, with 77 participants positively noting the explanations provided.
findings.measure: Observed content errors with misconception potential; participant qualitative feedback on explanations

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods pre/post study with n=102, but it relies heavily on self-reported perceptions and lacks an objective learning test or randomized comparison. The methodology supports useful primary evidence, though not at RCT/QED strength.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear positive shifts in perceptions and several large subgroup effect sizes, especially for GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5, but most outcomes are attitudinal and self-reported rather than validated academic achievement measures. Overall impact is promising but still unclear for direct learning gains.
